# Report Writing

> Copy of [Report Writing](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes/blob/main/docs/report-writing.md) from [Intelligence Field Notes](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes) 0.1.2. The original is the reference; this copy is here for offline use.

The report is the product. A chart, a graph, a folder of captures or a dashboard supports it, but the minimum analytical product is a written report: that is one of the UNODC manual's ten standards for analysts, and ICD 203 asks for "a clear main analytic message up front". This page covers the structure, the rules of the prose and a checklist before release.

## Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF)
Put the answer first. The reader may stop after the first paragraph; that paragraph must be enough to act on.
- **The first section answers the question that was asked**, in three to five sentences: what you found, what it means, how sure you are.
- **The first sentence of every paragraph covers the whole paragraph**, like an umbrella. The sentences after it support it, from the most important to the least. If a sentence does not fit under the umbrella, it belongs in another paragraph, or the first sentence is wrong.
- **Write the bottom line last.** Draft the findings, then write the summary that covers them, then check that every finding sits under it.
- **Never open on a date or on how something began.** "The group first appeared in 2023" covers nothing. Open on what the reader must take away; the history goes last, if at all.

## Structure
A standard shape for an OSINT or investigative report. Shorter products (an alert, a one-page brief) keep the first two sections and fold the rest into a few lines.

1.  **Header:** title, case reference, analyst, date (UTC), version number, handling marking (for example `TLP:AMBER`).
2.  **Bottom line:** the question and the answer (see above).
3.  **Key judgements:** numbered, each one sentence, each with its likelihood or confidence and the sources it rests on.
4.  **Findings:** the facts established, numbered, each with its source references and grades (`S3, B2`). Facts and judgements are kept apart (see below).
5.  **Analysis:** how the findings support the judgements; the alternatives considered and why they were rejected; key assumptions.
6.  **Gaps and next steps:** what you could not establish, what would close each gap, and the indicators that would change the judgements.
7.  **Recommendations** (only if asked for): the actions, kept in their own section and nowhere else.
8.  **Sources:** a table with reference, description, URL or origin, capture date and time (UTC), grade, and SHA-256 of the capture.
9.  **Method and limitations:** tools and versions, collection window, environment and OPSEC level, what was not searched and why.
10. **Annexes:** charts, timelines, maps, screenshots, raw extracts.

If the report changes the judgement of an earlier one, say so in the bottom line and explain why (tradecraft standard 7).

## Facts, Assumptions and Judgements
The reader must always know which is which.
- **Facts** are what you observed and captured. State them plainly, with the source: "The domain was registered on 3 May 2026 (S4, A1)."
- **Assumptions** are suppositions you use to frame or bridge the argument. State them as assumptions, especially when the argument depends on them.
- **Judgements** are conclusions drawn from the facts and assumptions. Mark them with the [estimative language](estimative-language.md): a likelihood term for events, a confidence level for the judgement, never both in one sentence.

A useful discipline is to label, at least in your draft, every claim as *observed* or *inferred*. A claim you cannot label observed is inferred, or you do not make it.

## Sourcing in the Text
- Every finding carries its reference to the Sources table (`S1`, `S2`...) and its 4 x 4 grade (see [Source Evaluation](source-evaluation.md)).
- Describe the source base honestly once, in a sentence or two: how many independent sources, of which kinds, and which ones the key judgements depend on (ICD 206 calls this a *source summary statement*).
- Never present a tool output, a search result count or an AI summary as a source. Cite the record behind it.

## How the Prose Is Written
The rules below are drawn from the CIA *Style Manual & Writers Guide for Intelligence Publications* (chapter 9) and the BLUF guidance used in US intelligence training.
- **One sentence, one claim.** Aim for about twenty words; treat thirty-five as the ceiling. If a sentence holds two things that could each stand alone, it is two sentences.
- **Active voice, with the actor as subject.** "The affiliates exploited the VPN appliance", not "the appliance was observed being exploited".
- **Concrete over vague.** Name the specifics instead of "various", "several", "multiple", "a number of". If you do not have the specifics, delete the phrase: "across sectors" claims less than "across multiple sectors" and says as much.
- **Close every list.** No "etc.", "and more", "among others".
- **No hedged attribution.** Not "sources say", "it is believed", "reports suggest": cite the source or state the judgement with its estimative term.
- **No empty forecasting.** Not "it remains to be seen", "only time will tell".
- **Write about the subject, not about your sources.** "The article provides details of the activity" reviews your source; say what the details are.
- **Frugal with adjectives and adverbs.** Nouns and verbs carry the meaning; "unique", "unprecedented" and "critical" are almost always wrong.
- **Define acronyms** at first use; keep a glossary in long reports.
- **Consistent names and transliterations.** Choose one spelling for each person, organisation and place, give the original script at first mention when there is one, and keep to it.
- **Dates and times** unambiguous: `14 September 2026`, times in UTC with the local time in brackets when it matters.

## Handling and Redaction
- Mark the report with its handling level. The [Traffic Light Protocol 2.0](https://www.first.org/tlp/) is the common choice: `TLP:RED`, `TLP:AMBER+STRICT`, `TLP:AMBER`, `TLP:GREEN`, `TLP:CLEAR`.
- Include personal data only where the requirement needs it; redact the people who appear incidentally.
- Before pasting case text into an external AI service, remove the personal data first and restore it afterwards.

## Checklist Before Release
- [ ] Does the first paragraph answer the question that was asked?
- [ ] Could a reader act on the bottom line alone?
- [ ] Is every finding sourced and graded, and every source captured and hashed?
- [ ] Are facts, assumptions and judgements clearly told apart?
- [ ] Does every judgement use one likelihood row or a confidence level, never both in a sentence?
- [ ] Are the alternatives and the key assumptions stated?
- [ ] Are the gaps listed, with what would close them?
- [ ] Does the report say how it changes or confirms earlier reporting?
- [ ] Is the handling marking set, and is unnecessary personal data removed?
- [ ] Has someone else read it?

## Common Pitfalls
- Presenting an AI-generated summary, a matching score or a tool's verdict as analysis.
- Treating one account, channel or article as representative of a group or movement.
- Ignoring platform manipulation: bought followers, coordinated amplification, recycled content.
- Confusing what a source *claims* with what is *verified*.
- Padding: a short report that answers the question is finished; a long one that buries the answer is worse than short.
- Hiding the gaps to look complete. The reader will act on what you did not say.

## Templates
The SOsintOps workstations ship report templates built on this page: a plain Markdown template and Word templates for full and executive reports, profiles, event assessments and threat notices. See `templates/` in [Argos](https://github.com/SOsintOps/Argos) and [Speculator](https://github.com/SOsintOps/Speculator-Project).

## Further Reading
- **"Style Manual & Writers Guide for Intelligence Publications"** (CIA Directorate of Intelligence, 8th edition, 2011) - The house style of US analytic writing; chapter 9, the *Word Watchers List*, opens with the precepts (§9.3) behind the prose rules above. [PDF (FAS)](https://irp.fas.org/cia/product/style.pdf) · [PDF (The Black Vault)](https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/cia/cia-styleguide.pdf)
- **"How to Write an Intelligence Product in the Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) Format"** (US DOJ, National Drug Intelligence Center material, as used in teaching) - The umbrella paragraph, with a worked assessment. [PDF](https://courses.physics.illinois.edu/phys280/sp2022/docs-for-assignments/BLUF%20Writing%20Format.pdf)
- **"The Analyst's Style Manual"** (Mercyhurst College Institute for Intelligence Studies) - Analytic writing for students and practitioners. [PDF](https://ncirc.bja.ojp.gov/sites/ncirc/files/media/document/analysts_style_manual.pdf)
- **"Style Manual for Intelligence Production"** (Defense Intelligence Agency, 2016) - The DIA's production style. [PDF (governmentattic.org)](https://www.governmentattic.org/23docs/DIAstyleManualIntelProd_2016.pdf)
- **"ICD 203"** and **"ICD 206"** (ODNI) - Analytic standards and sourcing requirements. [ICD 203](https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-203.pdf) · [ICD 206](https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-206.pdf)
- **"Criminal Intelligence: Manual for Analysts"** (UNODC, 2011) - Chapter 11, presentation of results; chapter 5, the ten standards for analysts. [PDF](https://www.unodc.org/documents/organized-crime/Law-Enforcement/Criminal_Intelligence_for_Analysts.pdf)
- More on intelligence writing in the [Reading List](reading-list.md#intelligence-writing).
